episode_title: Are You Just One Version of Yourself?

stories.topic: How Jaipur Became The Pink City
stories.summary: Amit went to Jaipur and discovered that the 'pink city' label is not ancient at all. In 1876, the city was painted pink to commemorate a visit by Prince Albert, and it stuck — tourists came expecting pink, businesses painted everything pink to please them, and even those who rebelled against the pinkness ended up reinforcing it as the city's defining trait. Jaipur could have been ochre, multicoloured, anything — but a single accident locked in an identity for centuries.
stories.insight: Path dependence is destiny. A small accident deep in the past can disproportionately shape how a city — or a person — unfolds, because every reaction to it (conformity or rebellion) becomes another vote for the original identity.

stories.topic: The 14-Year-Old Girl Who Learned To Be Docile
stories.summary: Picture a fourteen-year-old Indian girl at a family gathering. She gets praised for her smile, for being charming, for being docile — what the toxic Marathi phrase 'bal gau jese' (just like a cow) captures perfectly. She learns that smiling and being pleasant wins approval, and that becomes her 'pinkness.' The persona she adopts to fit in eventually becomes who she believes she is, foreclosing the possibility of being bold, ambitious, or assertive.
stories.insight: Childhood praise is a covert programming language. Innocent-seeming social validation in early years lays down behaviours that, over decades, calcify into identity — and the trap is most dangerous because the person never realises she chose it.

stories.topic: 'Have You Ever Shouted At Anyone?' — The Listener Who Knew Only One Amit
stories.summary: At a book launch, a sweet listener — a regular of The Seen and the Unseen — came up to Amit with her husband and asked, with full sincerity, 'Have you ever shouted at someone in your life?' She knew Amit only as the calm, articulate, thoughtful voice in her ears, and assumed that was all of him. Amit felt terrible, realising that the persona he projects on the show, however authentic, is just one slice of him — but for thousands of listeners, that slice has become the whole.
stories.insight: The danger of building an audience is that you get flattened into one dimension. Every public-facing creator's persona is necessarily partial, but listeners (and you) start to believe it is total — and the multitudes become invisible even to yourself.

stories.topic: Fox News Could Not Tell The Truth About The 2020 Election
stories.summary: When Fox News initially tried to report the truth about the 2020 US presidential election — that Trump had lost — its viewers fled in alarming numbers, threatening the network's business model. So Fox made a literal business decision to carry the stolen-election conspiracy theories to keep the audience. The leader had become a prisoner of the followers: when the followers no longer recognise you, you are no longer a leader.
stories.insight: Audience capture is a structural fact, not a moral failing. Once a brand or a person stakes out a tribe, the financial and social incentives to stay 'in character' overwhelm any private commitment to truth — the person and the persona stop being distinguishable.

stories.topic: The Tolstoy Chicken — A Lesson In Seen And Unseen
stories.summary: In old age, Tolstoy was a self-righteous moralist preaching against eating animals. His aunt, even older and uninterested in his lectures, declared she was coming to dinner and demanded chicken. So Tolstoy seated her at the table — with a live, squawking chicken on her chair. 'You wanted a chicken, there's your chicken. Have it.' Amit wrote an essay on this in the late nineties: there is a moral chasm between the chicken on the chair and the chicken on the plate, and our cuisine depends on never seeing the first.
stories.insight: Most ethics is downstream of distance. The reason we tolerate (in fact, savour) what we would never personally do is that we never see the unseen step in the chain — and a single live chicken on a chair collapses an entire ideology of polite consumption.

stories.topic: Even Fruit Flies Mourn Their Dead
stories.summary: Recent experiments showed that fruit flies — among the most basic creatures we can experiment on — exposed to the sight of dead fruit flies suffered a measurable shortening of their own lifespan. Not just mammals, not just birds, not just intelligent creatures: the moral injury of witnessing death goes all the way down to flies.
stories.insight: If sentience and grief reach this far down the tree of life, the ethical weight on our food choices is heavier than we admit. Lab-grown meat isn't a fad — it could be the technology that finally lets us eat well without participating in suffering we are biologically wired to recognise even in flies.

stories.topic: The Indian Lawyer Who Expected Murli To Lie
stories.summary: Murli Neelakantan, after a long career as a partner in UK and US law firms, came back to India and took on an Indian client. The client expected Murli, as a lawyer, to lie on his behalf — that's just how it works here. In the West, perjury is the rare exception that ends a career. In India, it is so normalised that clients are surprised when their lawyer refuses.
stories.insight: A profession's dharma is not what its members write in their oath, but what its surrounding institutions demand and tolerate. When the institutional environment rewards perjury and punishes principle, the dharma drifts — and the few who hold the line look like fools.

stories.topic: Lancelot Pinto's Paracetamol vs. Death By Over-Treatment
stories.summary: When Amit got COVID, Dr. Lancelot Pinto prescribed paracetamol and a throat gargle — and that was it. Lancelot's view, shared by other doctors like the liver doctor Abby Phillips, is that during COVID a significant share of deaths came from over-treatment: panicked patients demanding ivermectin and steroids and antibiotics from their doctors, and triggering cytokine storms in the second week. The doctor's dharma is to heal, but his incentive is to give the patient what the patient demands.
stories.insight: The deepest conflict in any caring profession is between the dharma (do what is right for the person in front of you) and the market (give them what they ask for). Without institutional spine — peers, regulators, malpractice cost — the market wins, and the patient's misinformed wish becomes their cause of death.

recommendations.item: Classical Liberalism — A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: An introductory book by Eamonn Butler of the IEA, available free as PDF and as a cheap Kindle edition.
recommendations.reason: Amit's argument: most of the ideas we absorb by osmosis when young are wrong but feel virtuous (the soft socialism of 'social justice' that quietly relies on state coercion). Butler's primers are an antidote — short, free, and crystal-clear introductions to the ideas Amit has spent his career writing about. 'These books are an education, and it is a miracle that they are free.'

recommendations.item: Friedrich Hayek: The Ideas and Influence of the Libertarian Economist
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Butler's primer on Hayek.
recommendations.reason: Hayek's own books can be heavy going; Butler distils him for the curious newcomer who wants the core ideas without the apparatus.

recommendations.item: Ludwig von Mises — A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Butler's primer on Mises.
recommendations.reason: An accessible doorway into Austrian economics for readers who do not want to start with Human Action.

recommendations.item: Milton Friedman: A Concise Guide to the Ideas and Influence of the Free-Market Economist
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Butler's primer on Friedman.
recommendations.reason: Friedman is the bridge between academic economics and public life; Butler's primer is the cleanest short path into him.

recommendations.item: Public Choice — A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Butler's primer on the public-choice school of Buchanan and Tullock.
recommendations.reason: Both Amit and Ajay are passionate about public choice theory — the insight that politicians and bureaucrats are self-interested actors, not benevolent stewards. Buchanan and Tullock's originals are dense; Butler delivers the framework directly. Foundational for the whole episode's argument about institutional design.

recommendations.item: Adam Smith — A Primer
recommendations.creator: Eamonn Butler
recommendations.context: Butler's primer on Adam Smith.
recommendations.reason: Smith is more than the invisible hand; the primer recovers the moral philosopher behind the economist.

recommendations.item: Lifespan: Why We Age — and Why We Don't Have To
recommendations.creator: David Sinclair
recommendations.context: Sinclair's book on extending healthy human lifespan well past one hundred.
recommendations.reason: Recommended in tandem with Roshan Abbas as the corrective to the assumption that long life means decades of dementia. Sinclair argues for compressed morbidity — vitality stretched, decline shortened. Without this premise, Ajay's 'extended lifespan = extended possibility' frame collapses.

recommendations.item: Outlive: The Science and Art of Longevity
recommendations.creator: Peter Attia
recommendations.context: Attia's book on longevity, listed in the show notes alongside Sinclair.
recommendations.reason: Attia is the practical companion to Sinclair: less the science of why we age and more the daily protocol for how to age well.

recommendations.item: The Nurture Assumption: Why Children Turn Out the Way They Do
recommendations.creator: Judith Rich Harris
recommendations.context: A seminal social-science book Amit calls one of the most important of the last century.
recommendations.reason: Harris's evidence that parents matter far less than peers and genes in shaping who children become. Amit raises it as a tangent (Ajay pushes back, citing assortative mating); promised as the subject of a future episode. Read it because it overturns the entire 'good parenting' industry.

recommendations.item: Reforms of Prosecution in the Indian Criminal Justice System
recommendations.creator: Smriti Parsheera
recommendations.context: A blog post on the Leap Journal by Smriti Parsheera, who worked with Ajay at NIPFP.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's recommendation for anyone who wants to go deeper into the broken state of the Indian public prosecutor's office — the institution that has 'withered away' over the years and needs to be revived.

recommendations.item: FSLRC Report and Draft Indian Financial Code
recommendations.creator: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission
recommendations.context: The FSLRC's full report and the draft Indian Financial Code that emerged from it.
recommendations.reason: Ajay points to the FSLRC machinery as the one Indian context where a fully articulated investigation-prosecution-adjudication regime has been worked out — a worked example for how a regulator like SEBI could be redesigned with proper checks and balances.

recommendations.item: Murli Neelakantan Looks at the World (Episode 329, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Murli Neelakantan
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with the lawyer Murli Neelakantan.
recommendations.reason: The conversation that surfaced the contrast between the Western and Indian dharma of a lawyer — perjury as career-ender vs. perjury as expected service to the client.

recommendations.item: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Dr. Lancelot Pinto.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Lancelot articulated the doctor's dharma and the over-treatment problem during COVID — a case study in how patient demand corrupts medical practice.

recommendations.item: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Abby Philips
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the liver doctor Abby Philips.
recommendations.reason: Another vector on the same problem of medical mis-incentives — a doctor who has staked his career on calling out quackery.

recommendations.item: Gurwinder Bhogal Examines Human Nature (Episode 331, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Gurwinder Bhogal
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Gurwinder Bhogal.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Amit picked up the 'looking-glass self' framing he uses in this conversation. Bhogal is a sharp psychologist of internet behaviour.

recommendations.item: Suyash Rai Embraces India's Complexity (Episode 307, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Suyash Rai.
recommendations.reason: Suyash is the originating mind for several themes in this episode: the dharma framing, the warning against treating the state as either necessary or sufficient, and the line that we are each a 'linear combination of our influences.'

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The Ukraine deep-dive Amit and Ajay did on The Seen and the Unseen.
recommendations.reason: The episode that triggered Ajay shaving his beard — Putin's 'bearded intellectuals oppose the war' line was the prompt.

recommendations.item: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas.
recommendations.reason: Roshan Abbas is the source of the '120-year life' provocation that Amit re-tells here — the same idea that frames the longevity recommendations.

recommendations.item: The Secret World Beneath Our Feet Is Mind-Blowing — And The Key To Our Planet's Future
recommendations.creator: George Monbiot
recommendations.context: Monbiot's Guardian piece on the soil microbiome.
recommendations.reason: The intellectual ground for Ajay's anti-recommendation of hydroponics. Monbiot's argument: the half-metre of soil under our feet is the most important and least understood ecosystem on the planet, and industrial agriculture (and hydroponics) is destroying it.

recommendations.item: Seeing Dead Fruit Flies Is Bad For The Health Of Fruit Flies
recommendations.creator: Christi Gendron
recommendations.context: A research write-up on Gendron's lab study showing fruit flies exposed to dead fruit flies have shortened lifespans.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's closing data point: moral injury from witnessing death goes all the way down to flies. The implication is enormous — if even fruit flies grieve, the case for lab-grown meat is not just sentimental but ethically and biologically grounded.

recommendations.item: Beautiful Boy
recommendations.creator: John Lennon
recommendations.context: Lennon's lullaby for his son Sean, source of the line 'Life is what happens to you while you're busy making other plans.'
recommendations.reason: Amit reaches for the line to capture the limits of agency — that we should not exaggerate our capacity to curate our circumstances. The show notes also point to a Paul McCartney video listening to the song and remembering John, recommended as a tender artefact.

recommendations.item: The Looking-Glass Self
recommendations.creator: Charles Cooley
recommendations.context: Charles Cooley's classic sociological concept.
recommendations.reason: We shape ourselves by how we believe others see us. Hanging out with Ajay, Amit will unconsciously cut the dad jokes and elevate the econ. The choice we have is therefore not 'who am I' but 'whose mirror do I stand in front of.'

core_ideas.concept: The Pinkness of Jaipur (Path Dependence in People)
core_ideas.explanation: The world is not a tidy equilibrium. Small accidents — a prince's visit in 1876, a praise from an aunt at a family gathering, a viral tweet — get amplified into identities that lock in for decades. Tourists and locals both reinforce Jaipur's pinkness because the incentives all point that way; even rebellion against the identity reinforces it. The same machinery operates inside a person: a persona adopted to win approval becomes self-reinforcing, and the mask becomes the face.
core_ideas.quote: Jaipur could have been many things, but it became a pink city.

core_ideas.concept: The Mukhota Becomes The Mukh (Mask Becomes Face)
core_ideas.explanation: A persona starts as a strategy for fitting in or succeeding in one context. Once adopted, it gets validated, and the validation makes you double down. Audiences expect that version of you — listeners, followers, clients, family. Changing the persona starts to feel like betrayal, and the gap between the public self and the private multitude widens until the multitude becomes inaccessible even to you. The danger is not adopting personas; it is forgetting they are personas.

When a creator, channel or institution stakes out a tribe, the tribe's expectations become a financial and social cage. Fox News could not tell its viewers Trump lost without losing the viewers; a YouTuber known for one hot take cannot quietly change his mind without bleeding subscribers. The leader is bound by the followers — without followers, she is not a leader. Modern social-media incentives (likes, subscribers, ad revenue, ego) make audience capture nearly impossible to escape once you have an audience worth capturing.
core_ideas.quote: If the followers are not there, then suddenly she is not a leader anymore.

core_ideas.concept: We Are Linear Combinations Of Our Influences
core_ideas.explanation: Suyash Rai's frame: each of us is a weighted average of the people around us. The looking-glass self (Cooley) and mimetic desire (Girard) describe the same machinery from different angles — we shape ourselves by how others see us, and we want what those near us want. The implication is not that you have a true self underneath; the truer move is to choose your inputs carefully. Curate the five, fifteen, fifty people whose opinions you absorb. After that, the math takes over.
core_ideas.quote: We are each of us a linear combination of our influences.

core_ideas.explanation: In the old world, life expectancy at twenty was about sixty-five — one adult life, one company, one costume. A twenty-year-old today has potentially a hundred years ahead. That is enough time for many sequential lives — banker, then writer, then activist, then teacher. The right question shifts from 'what will I be' to 'what do I want to become in the next twenty years' — answered, and asked again, every two decades. Even if you only have twenty years left, behaving as if you have fifty changes the texture of your daily decisions.
core_ideas.quote: If you carry this idea deep into your head and you think hey, I have fifty years to go — that is the greatest headroom of all.

core_ideas.concept: Self-Awareness As The Only Liberation From Social Programming
core_ideas.explanation: Every human is the product of social programming — childhood praise, cultural cues, random reinforcement. You cannot will it away or wish it away. The only escape is becoming conscious of it: an AI that begins to interrogate its own operating system. This is precisely what the current LLMs cannot do, and what humans uniquely can. Examined life, examined operating system. Without it, you are running someone else's code and calling it identity.
core_ideas.quote: It's like an AI that becomes conscious of its master, that understands the operating system it's been placed under.

core_ideas.concept: Confirmation Bias As An Investigator's Disease
core_ideas.explanation: The behavioural-economics finding: once you form a theory, the world rearranges itself to give you supporting evidence. This is not a failure of will; it is how the brain works. Investigators, prosecutors, journalists, scientists are all subject to it. The institutional answer is not to demand better people but to design checks: a separate prosecutor reviewing the investigator's case, a grand jury reviewing the prosecutor's case. Each layer is a forced collision with someone who does not share your pet theory.
core_ideas.quote: Once you have a point of view, the entire universe organizes itself to give you facts that enhance and support your belief.

core_ideas.explanation: Western legal systems evolved a multi-layer architecture for the decision to accuse a person of a crime: (1) investigator gathers evidence; (2) a separate public prosecutor decides whether the evidence meets the legal checklist for that crime, and is evaluated on conviction rate so frivolous cases hurt them; (3) a grand jury of citizens reviews the prosecutor's case before indictment. Each layer is fragile (juries can be deferential, citizens can be radicalised) but together they distribute the power to ruin a private life. India has none of this for many domains — SEBI, income tax, large parts of criminal justice — leaving complete executive discretion.
core_ideas.quote: Building the republic is this kind of unglamorous work — a 20-year, 40-year, 60-year journey.

core_ideas.explanation: When a government has unchecked power to indict, the indictment itself — independent of conviction — becomes the punishment. You spend years in court, lose reputation, exhaust savings, lose sleep. So why would a government in power dilute this tool? It is the most efficient instrument for harassing opponents. The honest answer Ajay gives is sobering: the laws were not fixed during the great reform window not because of evil but because of intellectual failures of people like himself — economists who lacked knowledge of law and public administration. The knowledge is finally accumulating now.
core_ideas.quote: If I am in government, I'm like — I got all the tools, man, I'm gonna punish everybody. Why would I dilute those tools?

core_ideas.concept: The Dharma Of A Profession (And How Institutions Shape It)
core_ideas.explanation: Every profession has a dharma — a doctor's is to heal, a lawyer's is to serve the law within the law, a journalist's is to speak truth to power. But the dharma is constantly in tension with the market: the patient demanding ivermectin, the client demanding perjury, the media owner demanding a partisan slant. Institutions tilt the balance one way or the other. UK law disbars perjurers and the dharma holds; Indian law tolerates perjury and the dharma drifts. Don't look to the state as the first or only enforcer — most of dharma is enforced by us, peer to peer, in the daily moral code we hold each other to.
core_ideas.quote: Don't look to the state as either necessary or sufficient. A lot of this happens between us as human beings.

core_ideas.concept: Winner Takes All And The Concentration Premium
core_ideas.explanation: Modern economies are increasingly winner-takes-all — a few people achieve disproportionate influence and shape an outsized share of the culture. The level of concentration required to break through is brutal, and people pursuing 'more prosaic objectives' run out of fuel before they get there. This is a hidden requirement of long, productive lives: you need a deeper-than-money source of motivation to sustain forty years of focused work. It is also a critique of careers organised around income alone — they peter out before they pay off.
core_ideas.quote: How do you stay hungry? How do you keep going? More prosaic objectives peter out.

core_ideas.concept: The Root Microbiome (Why Hydroponics Is A Mistake)
core_ideas.explanation: Just as the human gut microbiome — one to two kilograms of bacteria and yeast — produces complex chemicals our body needs, plants depend on a root microbiome in the soil for full nutritional richness. Hydroponics produces visually pristine vegetables (no insects, no soil grit) but at the cost of an impaired microbiome and systematically inferior nutrient profile. Same goes for over-tilled, fertilizer-drenched, pesticide-soaked industrial soil. The aesthetic of cleanliness in food is often a sign of nutritional emptiness.
core_ideas.quote: We should always favour the mess of true soil that has not been ploughed and that has not faced chemical fertilizers.

core_ideas.concept: Chicken On The Chair vs. Chicken On The Plate (Seen And Unseen In Ethics)
core_ideas.explanation: Tolstoy's prank — placing a live chicken on his aunt's dinner chair — is the seen-and-unseen of meat-eating in one image. We tolerate (and savour) consequences whose causes we have arranged never to see. Lab-grown meat is interesting because it short-circuits the contradiction: meat without the chicken on the chair. Fruit-fly evidence that even the lowest creatures suffer moral injury from witnessing death raises the stakes — sentience is wider than we admit, and the technology to escape participation in its violation is finally on the horizon.
core_ideas.quote: There's a difference that we ignore — it's a seen and the unseen, the chicken on the chair and the chicken on the plate.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay shaved his beard because Putin reportedly said 'everybody supports the invasion of Ukraine other than bearded intellectuals.' Amit's deadpan reply: 'Excuse me — Marx, Engels, Lenin, Trotsky? His own pantheon should be full of bearded intellectuals. What has he got against bearded intellectuals?'

Amit on the producer's intervention: 'Before we begin chapter two, my producer just told me to do something about my cleavage, so I've kind of buttoned my shirt together' — meta-humour about how even the hosts perform for the camera.

Amit, when Ajay asks how he would behave with five hundred years of life ahead: 'Dude, the show won't exist because I procrastinate so much.' Artificial urgency is the engine; remove the deadline and even the podcast disappears.
Amit, riffing on Lennon: 'Life is what happens to you while you're busy making podcasts.'
Amit on the limits of the leaf: 'Anybody who's eating a leaf, it's a superficial joy only. What joy can you get out of a leaf, no matter how it is grown?'
Amit fumbling: 'You can grow a chicken leg in a lamb. Not in a lamb. Don't try that at home. You can grow a chicken leg in a lab.'
Tolstoy seating his aunt at the dinner table with a live, squawking chicken on her chair: 'You wanted a chicken — there's your chicken. Have it.'
John Lennon, 'Beautiful Boy': 'Life is what happens to you when you're busy making other plans' — invoked to undercut our exaggerated sense of agency.
'Bal gau jese' — toxic Marathi phrase meaning 'just like a cow,' used to praise (and program) docility in girls.
'Mukhota becomes mukh' — Hindi/Marathi wordplay: the mask becomes the face. The episode's central line.
'You contain multitudes' — Whitman by way of the conversation, used as the antidote to the persona trap.

'If you are not a communist at eighteen you don't have a heart; if you are not a capitalist at twenty-eight you don't have a head' — the apocryphal saying Amit invokes when introducing the Butler primers on classical liberalism.
Looking-glass self (Charles Cooley) — picked up by Amit from his episode with Gurwinder Bhogal. We shape ourselves to the reflections we see in others' eyes.
Mimetic desire (Rene Girard) — we don't desire things independently; we desire what those around us desire.

Rabindranath Tagore's flowing beard — Amit's 'figure number one in my pantheon, because I'm half Bengali' — invoked against Putin's anti-bearded-intellectual line, with the note that Tagore would have opposed both this war and nationalism itself.
